Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### The District Court Properly Considered Documents Incorporated by Reference in the Complaint Without Converting the Rule 12(b)(6) Motion into One for Summary Judgment

#### A. Incorporated documents may be considered on a motion to dismiss without triggering Rule 12(d).

Rule 12(d) requires conversion to summary judgment only when "matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). This Court has long held that documents incorporated by reference into a complaint are not "outside the pleadings." "A court may . . . consider certain materials—documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by the complaint by reference, and matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003); *accord Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010). When a document is incorporated, the district court "may treat such a document as part of the complaint, and thus may assume that its contents are true for purposes of a motion to dismiss." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908.

The doctrine is settled in this Circuit. It reaches documents not physically attached to the complaint "if the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Id.* at 907; *see also Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). Earlier decisions reached the same result where the complaint alleges the document's contents and no party questions its authenticity. *Branch v. Tunnell*, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119 (9th Cir. 2002); *Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006).

#### B. The doctrine extends to documents on which the claim depends, even if the complaint does not quote them.

This Court has extended incorporation by reference "to situations in which the plaintiff's claim depends on the contents of a document, the defendant attaches the document to its motion to dismiss, and the parties do not dispute the authenticity of the document, even though the plaintiff does not explicitly allege the contents of that document in the complaint." *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005). *See also Davis v. HSBC Bank Nev., N.A.*, 691 F.3d 1152, 1160 (9th Cir. 2012) (considering documents on which the complaint's allegations necessarily relied); *In re NVIDIA Corp. Sec. Litig.*, 768 F.3d 1046, 1058 n.10 (9th Cir. 2014) (considering documents incorporated by reference in the complaint).

The doctrine also serves an important purpose. It "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002. A plaintiff cannot avoid a document's full text by quoting it selectively or by relying on it without attaching it.

#### C. The district court's consideration of the documents here was proper.

Here, [Plaintiff's] claims rest on [the Agreement / the disclosures / the website content] (the "Documents"). The Complaint refers to the Documents [__ times] and quotes them at paragraphs [__]. [ER __.] Because the claims "depend[] on the contents" of the Documents, they were properly incorporated. *Knievel*, 393 F.3d at 1076; *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 907. Defendant submitted the Documents with its motion, and Plaintiff did not question their authenticity below. [ER __.] The district court therefore acted within its discretion in treating the Documents as part of the Complaint. *Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448.

Nor did the court use the Documents to resolve factual disputes against Plaintiff. *Khoja* cautions that "it is improper to assume the truth of an incorporated document if such assumptions only serve to dispute facts stated in a well-pleaded complaint." 899 F.3d at 1003. The district court observed that limit. It relied on the Documents for what they say, not to contradict any well-pleaded allegation. [ER __.] Where the Complaint's characterization of a document is contradicted by the document's actual text, the court need not accept the characterization. The court's reading of the Documents' plain terms was a legal determination appropriate at the pleading stage, not a weighing of evidence.

Because the Documents were incorporated by reference, they were not "matters outside the pleadings," and Rule 12(d) did not require conversion. *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908. This Court should affirm.
